description: Curated life-situation topics for the Explore section. Verse mappings are editorial choices, never computed at request time. Currently mapped only to the development placeholder verses; full curation follows the verified dataset.

licenses.name: In-house editorial content
licenses.notes: Original prose written for this product. Not scripture.

sources.name: In-house topic curation
sources.verificationNotes: Editorial introductions and verse mappings written for this product. Needs review by someone with the relevant scholarly background before publication.

topics.name: Anger
topics.shortDescription: Where anger comes from, and what the Gita suggests doing about it.
topics.introduction: The Gita does not treat anger as a moral failing to be ashamed of. It treats it as the end of a chain that starts much earlier - in what the mind keeps returning to. That is useful, because it means the place to intervene is upstream of the anger itself.

verses.note: The chain: dwelling on objects, attachment, desire, anger.

topics.name: Fear
topics.shortDescription: Fear of loss, of failure, of death - and the ground the Gita offers under it.
topics.introduction: Much of what is called fear is fear of losing something. The Gita's response is not reassurance that nothing will be lost. It is a claim about what cannot be lost, and a reframing of duty that does not depend on the outcome being safe.

verses.note: What is not destroyed when the body is.
Another's duty, however attractive, brings danger.

topics.name: Anxiety
topics.shortDescription: The restlessness of a mind rehearsing outcomes it cannot control.
topics.introduction: Anxiety usually lives in the future tense. The Gita's central practical instruction - a claim on the action, not on the fruit - is aimed exactly there. It does not promise outcomes will be good. It relocates where your effort belongs.

verses.note: The claim is on the action, never on the fruit.

topics.name: Stress
topics.shortDescription: Pressure, overwork, and the question of what is actually yours to carry.
topics.introduction: Stress often comes from carrying two things at once: the work, and the verdict on the work. The Gita separates them, and is unusually practical about moderation in eating, sleeping and working as part of the same discipline.

verses.note: Separating the work from the verdict on the work.

topics.name: Grief
topics.shortDescription: The Gita begins in grief; it does not begin by dismissing it.
topics.introduction: The entire dialogue is occasioned by grief. Arjuna's despondency is given a full chapter before any answer is offered, and the answer, when it comes, is about what persists.

verses.note: The setting in which the grief arises.
Change of body compared to change of age.
That which is not born and does not die.

topics.name: Jealousy
topics.shortDescription: Comparison, and the confusion of another's path with your own.
topics.introduction: Jealousy assumes that someone else's role would have been better for you. The Gita's answer is svadharma: your own work, imperfectly done, is still the work that is yours.

verses.note: One's own duty, imperfect, over another's done well.

topics.name: Loneliness
topics.shortDescription: Being alone, and the self as its own companion.
topics.introduction: The Gita's response to isolation is unexpectedly self-reliant: it points to a relationship with oneself before pointing anywhere else.

verses.note: The self as its own friend, or its own enemy.

topics.name: Confusion
topics.shortDescription: Not knowing what the right thing to do is.
topics.introduction: Arjuna's problem is not weakness of will. He genuinely cannot see which action is right - every option violates something he holds. This is the condition the Gita is addressed to.

verses.note: The two sides, and the question that opens the dialogue.
A criterion when several courses look defensible.

topics.name: Attachment
topics.shortDescription: Holding on, and what holding on costs.
topics.introduction: Attachment in the Gita is not affection. It is the dependence of your steadiness on a particular outcome, and it is described as the hinge on which desire and anger turn.

verses.note: Attachment as the step between dwelling and desire.
Non-attachment to the fruit, without withdrawal from the work.

topics.name: Lack of motivation
topics.shortDescription: When the work feels pointless, or too heavy to start.
topics.introduction: The Gita takes seriously the state of not wanting to act, and answers it twice: first that inaction is not actually available, and second that the self can lift itself.

verses.note: Lift yourself by yourself.
Where effort properly belongs.

topics.name: Career
topics.shortDescription: Choosing work, and doing it without being consumed by it.
topics.introduction: The Gita's vocabulary for work - svadharma, karma-yoga, the fruit of action - maps onto career questions unusually well, provided you do not read it as advice to stop caring.

verses.note: Your own work over a more prestigious one.
Effort and outcome, separated.

topics.name: Business
topics.shortDescription: Enterprise, risk and the discipline of not being ruled by results.
topics.introduction: Building something means living with uncertain outcomes for long stretches. The Gita's framing gives a way to stay engaged without being governed by the quarterly verdict.

verses.note: Sustained effort without dependence on the result.

topics.name: Studies
topics.shortDescription: Learning, examinations, and steadiness under evaluation.
topics.introduction: For a student, the gap between effort and result is unusually visible. That is exactly the gap the Gita addresses.

verses.note: The claim is on preparation, not on the mark.
Self-reliance in study.

topics.name: Failure
topics.shortDescription: When it did not work, and what that does and does not mean about you.
topics.introduction: If your worth is attached to the outcome, failure is an identity event. The Gita's separation of action from fruit is, among other things, a way of surviving it.

verses.note: Outcome was never the part you owned.
Do not let yourself sink.

topics.name: Success
topics.shortDescription: Doing well without being owned by it.
topics.introduction: The Gita treats success and failure with the same instruction, which is a stronger claim than it first appears: equanimity is not only for the bad days.

verses.note: The same footing in success as in failure.

topics.name: Relationships
topics.shortDescription: Duty, affection and conflict with the people closest to you.
topics.introduction: Arjuna's crisis is a relationship crisis: the people on the other side are his teachers and cousins. The Gita does not resolve this by making the relationships matter less.

verses.note: Kinsmen on both sides.

topics.name: Money
topics.shortDescription: Wealth as an instrument, and the trouble of treating it as the point.
topics.introduction: The Gita is not ascetic about wealth. It is precise about what happens when acquisition becomes the aim rather than the means.

verses.note: How wanting escalates.

topics.name: Leadership
topics.shortDescription: Responsibility for others, and setting the standard by what you do.
topics.introduction: The Gita's account of leadership is behavioural: people follow what the capable person actually does, not what they recommend.

verses.note: Doing your own work rather than a more visible one.

topics.name: Decision making
topics.shortDescription: Choosing when the options are all costly.
topics.introduction: The Gita's situation is not a choice between good and bad. It is a choice between two things that both violate something. That is what makes it useful.

verses.note: A criterion when several courses look defensible.
The shape of the dilemma.

topics.name: Discipline
topics.shortDescription: Practice, repetition, and a mind that will not sit still.
topics.introduction: The Gita is candid that the mind is hard to steady, and answers with two words rather than encouragement: practice and dispassion.

verses.note: Self-effort as the mechanism.

topics.name: Purpose
topics.shortDescription: What your work is for.
topics.introduction: Purpose in the Gita is closer to fit than to ambition: the work that is yours, done in the right spirit, rather than the most impressive work available.

verses.note: Svadharma stated directly.

topics.name: Duty
topics.shortDescription: Dharma: obligation that does not depend on how you feel about it.
topics.introduction: Dharma is the Gita's central and least translatable term. It is not law, and not preference. It is what is genuinely yours to do, given who and where you are.

verses.note: Svadharma over paradharma.
How duty is to be performed.
Dharma as something that can decline and be restored.

topics.name: Death
topics.shortDescription: Mortality, and what the Gita says persists.
topics.introduction: The Gita's treatment of death is neither consoling nor evasive. It makes a claim about what is and is not destroyed, and lets the rest follow from that.

verses.note: Death as a change of body, like a change of age.
Unborn, everlasting, not slain when the body is slain.

topics.name: Meditation
topics.shortDescription: Sitting, steadying, and what to do with a wandering mind.
topics.introduction: Chapter six is the practical one: where to sit, how much to eat and sleep, and what to do when the mind refuses. Krishna agrees that it is hard.

verses.note: The self as the instrument of its own steadying.

topics.name: Self-control
topics.shortDescription: Restraint that is not repression.
topics.introduction: The Gita's self-control is not suppression of feeling. It is the ability to not be moved by every impulse the senses report - which it describes as a skill, learned by practice.

verses.note: What happens without restraint.
The self as friend or enemy.
